This page records why the lab's notes write certain symbols the way they do.
Each entry states our convention, the reasons for it, and the other conventions you will meet in other sources.
Notes sites can link to an entry here instead of keeping their own copy.

## The vector mark {#sec-vector-mark}

Our convention is a tilde under the letter, as in $\vx$.
The shared macro `\vecf` (and shortcuts such as `\vx` and `\vbeta`) prints it.

We chose a mark underneath for three reasons.

-   Bold letters are hard to write by hand.
    When we work problems by hand, for example on a board, a bold letter is hard to copy neatly with chalk or a marker.
    A small tilde under a letter is quick to write, so the handwritten symbol and the printed symbol look the same.
-   The space above a letter is already used.
    In statistics, a hat over a symbol means "estimated value".
    A vector mark above the letter would have to share that space with the hat, and the two marks would be crowded together.
-   A mark below the letter stays in place when we add a hat.
    The vector mark stays below and the estimate mark stays above, so each mark can be read on its own.

::: {#exm-estimated-vector-notation}
##### An estimated vector

Suppose a regression model has a coefficient vector $\vbeta$ with $p$ entries.
Its estimate from data is written $\hvb$, with the hat above the symbol and the vector mark below it.
We read $\hvb$ as "the estimated vector $\vbeta$".
Its $j$-th entry is the estimate of the $j$-th coefficient.
That entry is a single number, so it needs no vector mark, only the hat.
:::

Other sources use bold letters ($\mathbf{x}$) or arrows ($\overrightarrow{x}$) for the same objects.
All of these notations mark a vector.

## Subscripts and parentheses {#sec-subscripts-parentheses}

Our convention splits the work between a subscript and parentheses.
An indexed family is a collection of objects labeled by an index.
A subscript names which member of an indexed family we mean.
A subscript holds an index, such as the $i$ in $x_i$,
or a parameter that picks one function or distribution out of a family, such as the $\theta$ in $f_\theta$.
Parentheses hold the input a function is evaluated at, as in $f(x)$.
So $f_\theta(x)$ reads "the member of the family labeled $\theta$, evaluated at $x$".

We chose this split for one reason.
Each slot then answers one question about the symbol, so once you know the split, you can tell what each part of a symbol is doing.

Nothing forces the split.
Sources divide the work differently, and you will meet the same objects written the other way around.
When you read a formula from another source, first work out what each subscript and each input in parentheses is doing:
labeling a member of an indexed family, or being the input of a function.
That tells you which convention the source follows, whatever its layout.

::: {#exm-stochastic-process-slots}
##### A stochastic process uses both slots

A random experiment is a process that involves chance, such as a coin flip, and an outcome $\omega$ is one possible result of it.
A random variable is a function whose input is an outcome $\omega$.
A stochastic process is an indexed family of random variables $X_t$, one for each index $t$, such as a time.
The index goes in the subscript, because it picks a member of the family.
Each $X_t$ is itself a function of the outcome $\omega$, so the outcome goes in the parentheses: $X_t(\omega)$.
Fixing $\omega$ and letting $t$ vary gives one ordinary function of $t$, called a path of the process.
Many sources drop $\omega$ and write $X_t$.
Others write $X(t)$, often when $t$ is continuous, which puts the index in the parentheses instead of the subscript.
:::

## Binary labels {#sec-binary-labels}

A binary classification problem has two classes, and each observation carries a label that names its class.
Our convention is to code the labels as $0$ and $1$, as in logistic regression, where the label $1$ means the event happened.
The chapter on support vector machines switches to the labels $-1$ and $+1$, and says so where it does.

We switch to $-1$ and $+1$ for support vector machines for one reason.
With $\pm 1$ labels, a prediction is correct exactly when the model's output and the label have the same sign, so the product of the label and the output is positive for a correct prediction and negative for a wrong one.
Its size says how far the point sits from the decision boundary.
With $0$ and $1$ labels, the same test needs two cases.

Both codings describe the same data.
Other sources pick one coding and use it everywhere, so check which one a formula assumes before comparing it with ours.

## The intercept {#sec-intercept}

A linear model for an outcome adds up the inputs times their coefficients, and then adds one more number that does not multiply any input.
That number is the intercept.
Our convention is to write the intercept separately, as $\coef{0}$, and to let the coefficient vector $\vcoef$ hold the slopes only.
So a score is written $\coef{0} + \dprod{\vcoef}{\vpredvar}$.

Writing it separately has one benefit.
Formulas such as the decision boundary of logistic regression treat the intercept differently from the slopes, and showing $\coef{0}$ keeps that visible.

Other sources absorb the intercept.
They add a constant input $1$ to the start of the input vector and put the intercept at the start of the coefficient vector.
The score is then $\dprod{\vcoef}{\vpredvar}$ alone.
Both forms describe the same model.
When you meet a score written as $\dprod{\vcoef}{\vpredvar}$, check whether the input vector starts with a constant $1$.

## Counting the layers of a neural network {#sec-counting-layers}

A neural network passes its input through a sequence of layers.
Suppose a network has an input layer, one hidden layer (a layer between the input and the output), and an output layer.
Some sources call it a three-layer network, because it has three rows of units.
Our convention is to call it a two-layer network, because it has two weight matrices: input to hidden, and hidden to output.
We can also say that it has one hidden layer.

We count the weight matrices because the input layer holds no parameters and does no computation.
It is the data.
Counting the transformations therefore counts the layers that do work.

Both names are in use.
Check which one a source means before comparing the depths of two networks.

## Conventions for cross-entropy {#sec-cross-entropy-conventions}

Cross-entropy is a measure of how well a model's predicted probabilities match the observed labels.
Two choices change its numerical value without changing which of two models it prefers.

The first choice is the base of the logarithm.
The definition leaves the base free, so state it whenever you quote a number.
Base $e$ measures cross-entropy in nats, and base $2$ measures it in bits.
A two-class model that has learned nothing scores $\log_e 2 \approx 0.693$ per example in nats and $\log_2 2 = 1$ per example in bits.
Changing the base multiplies every score by the same positive constant, so it cannot change which of two classifiers you would pick.
It does change the number, so a cross-entropy quoted without its base cannot be checked against a number from another source.

The second choice is whether to sum or to average over the examples.
Our convention is to sum over all examples, and to say so wherever it matters.
Most software reports the average under the same name.
Check which one a source reports before comparing its numbers with ours.

## Weights and coefficients, dimension, sample size and targets {#sec-ml-statistics-names}

Machine learning and statistics developed their notations separately, and the same object often has two names and two symbols.
Our convention is to pick the symbols that fit the chapter, and to say which ones a chapter uses.
For example, the chapter on neural networks writes $\vw$ and $b$, and the regression chapters write $\vcoef$ and $\beta_0$.

-   A linear function is written $f(\vx) = \dprod{\vw}{\vx} + b$ in neural network texts, where $\vw$ holds the weights and $b$ is the bias, which plays the role of the intercept.
    Statistics texts write the coefficients as $\vbeta$ and the intercept as $\beta_0$.
    These are the same linear model.
-   Machine learning texts often write the dimension of the input as $D$ or $d$ and the number of observations as $N$.
    Statistics texts write the number of observations as $n$ and the number of predictors as $p$.
-   Neural network and pattern recognition texts often call the label the target and write it $t$ or $y$.
    Statistics calls it the response or the outcome and writes it $y$.

We keep both sets of symbols because you will read both literatures.
